lesson.title: The Control Plane: Deciding Before Delivering
lesson.summary: The control plane is the part of a network responsible for figuring out where traffic should go, building the routing information that the data plane then uses to actually forward every packet, whether that logic lives inside each router or is centralized the way SDN does it.
lesson.body:
Routing protocols like OSPF and BGP are the clearest, most concrete example of control plane work: routers exchange information with their neighbors about what networks they can reach, run an algorithm to compute the best path to each destination from that information, and use the result to build a routing table. All of that, the neighbor exchanges, the path computation, the table building, is the control plane. It is the part of the system doing the figuring out. Whatever eventually happens to the actual data packets streaming through the router, millions of them per second on a busy link, is a separate concern: the data plane, whose entire job is to look up a destination in an already-built table and forward the packet accordingly, as fast as possible, without recomputing anything.

The SDN chapter introduced this split as software-defined networking's central idea: pulling the control plane out of individual devices and centralizing it in a controller. But the control plane versus data plane distinction is not itself an SDN invention, SDN simply relocates where the control plane runs. In a traditional router, the control plane and data plane both live inside the same box, but they are still conceptually distinct pieces of work happening at very different rates: the control plane reacts to relatively rare events, a neighbor announcing a new route, a link going down, while the data plane executes constantly, on every single packet, using whatever forwarding table the control plane most recently produced. In practice, a router typically compiles the control plane's routing table, often called the RIB, into a separate, faster-to-look-up forwarding table, the FIB, that the data plane actually consults, which is one reason the two can be reasoned about almost independently even when they live in the same physical device.

A concrete example makes the volume difference vivid. A BGP session between two internet service providers' routers is entirely control plane traffic: a comparatively small number of messages exchanged periodically, or whenever reachability changes, announcing which address prefixes each provider can deliver traffic to. That session has nothing to do with the millions of customer packets per second actually crossing that same router at the same time, streaming video, web requests, and everything else, which is data plane traffic, forwarded using the FIB the control plane already computed, without consulting BGP again for each individual packet.

This separation also explains a distinct failure mode worth understanding on its own. If a router's control plane process becomes overloaded, or in an SDN network, if the centralized controller becomes unreachable, existing traffic does not necessarily stop immediately, because the data plane keeps forwarding packets using the last forwarding table it was given, which is still sitting there, still valid for now. What breaks is the network's ability to adapt: no new routes are learned, a failed link elsewhere does not get worked around, and the network effectively freezes into its last known state until the control plane recovers. That precise failure mode, forwarding continues on stale information while adaptation stops, is exactly why keeping the two concepts distinct matters operationally, and it is the deeper reason SDN's designers considered separating them worth the added complexity of a centralized controller in the first place.
